description: Set, lighting and sound choices that move between domestic interior and the symbolic garden of memory.
content_html:
Two Spaces, One Stage

The staging challenge at the heart of Things I Know to Be True is how to hold two fundamentally different spaces on stage simultaneously: the suburban kitchen, Fran’s practical domestic territory, and the rose garden, Bob’s emotional refuge. Both spaces must feel inhabited throughout the play; characters move between them, and that movement is always meaningful. A set design solution for this play must therefore do two things at once: establish the domestic realism of a contemporary Australian home and signal, through the choice of materials, levels and visual contrast, that the garden carries a weight beyond the literal.

Many production approaches use a largely bare stage with carefully chosen scenic elements: a kitchen table and chairs upstage to one side, a patch of soil or a single rose bush to the other. The simplicity prevents the design from competing with the play’s emotional register. The audience is asked to invest imaginatively in the spaces, and they will do so provided the key scenic signatures are clear: the hardness of the kitchen floor against the softness of the garden earth, the enclosed quality of the interior against the open expanse of the outdoor space.

Key Fact

The kitchen and the rose garden are the play’s twin centres. A designer’s task is to make them coexist on a shared stage while keeping their distinct qualities clear: the kitchen is practical and enclosed; the garden is open, symbolic and emotionally loaded.

Lighting the Seasons

Because the play moves through a full year in four seasons, a lighting designer has an unusually rich palette to work with. The seasonal arc creates a ready-made visual narrative: the lighting should track the emotional temperature of the play as much as the literal time of day. In spring, a warm, hopeful lighting state makes sense — perhaps a yellow-gold wash from a front-of-house wash bar, suggesting the optimism of new beginnings. By winter, the same space should feel colder and more exposed: a shift to a bluer, flatter wash, with reduced intensity, creates the emotional chill of the play’s ending without needing any text to announce it.

The garden, as an outdoor space, invites naturalistic lighting choices. Australian summer light is bright, high and unforgiving: a strong overhead source, perhaps a single profile lantern at steep angle to suggest midday sun, combined with a warm Fresnel fill from the side, would give the summer garden its harsh brightness. When the play moves into autumn and winter, the overhead angle softens; the fills are withdrawn. The physical sense of light shrinking is inseparable from the emotional sense of the family’s certainties contracting.

A gobo is one of the most versatile tools available to a lighting designer who needs to suggest organic, natural spaces on an otherwise bare stage. A leaf-break or branch-pattern gobo projected across the garden area would dapple the ground and the performers with shifting light and shadow, suggesting the presence of trees or foliage without any physical set element needing to represent it. In the spring and summer garden scenes, this gobo might be used with a warm amber gel; by autumn, the same gobo with an orange-red gel creates the impression of dying leaves. By winter, the gobo is withdrawn entirely: bare, flat light for a bare garden. The gobo therefore participates in the seasonal arc of the whole design.

Sound Design: Cicadas, Birdsong and the Kitchen Underscore

Sound design in this play must distinguish between two acoustic environments: the inside of the kitchen and the outside of the garden. This distinction is not just about realism; it is about the play’s emotional grammar. The kitchen is the space of direct confrontation — Fran’s world, where practical truths are spoken. The garden is the space of private feeling and slower time. A sound designer who understands this will create two distinct sonic environments and manage the transition between them carefully.

For the garden, a soundscape of cicadas and birdsong establishes the Australian summer setting while also carrying an emotional quality: the warmth and continuity of the natural world contrasting with the disruptions the children bring. As the seasons turn, the soundscape changes: autumn might bring a wind underscore, winter a near-silence broken only by rain. For the kitchen scenes, the sound design can afford to be more minimal — perhaps a low, barely perceptible underscore in the most emotionally charged confrontations, or simply the ambient sounds of a domestic interior: the distant hum of a refrigerator, the sound of water from a tap. These diegetic sounds ground the audience in the domestic reality of the space.

Key Fact

The sound design must create two distinct acoustic environments. The garden: a seasonal soundscape (cicadas in summer, wind in autumn, near-silence in winter). The kitchen: minimal underscore or diegetic domestic sounds. The shift between these environments should be part of every transition between the two spaces.

Costume Design: Season and Character

Costume in this play operates primarily in a naturalistic register: the Price family are a contemporary suburban Australian family, and their clothing should reflect that. Jeans, casual shirts, the particular textures of modern working life. However, the seasonal structure gives a costume designer the opportunity to make the passage of time visible through clothing. Pip’s spring arrival might be in light layers — linen or cotton in pale colours suggesting something new and tentative. Mark’s summer scenes might carry the heat of the season in warmer fabrics and colours. By winter, the clothing grows heavier, more protective.

The more significant costume choice concerns Mark’s arc as he transitions to Mia. The play tracks this across the summer season. A costume designer must collaborate closely with the director and, above all, with the performer to make choices that are specific, respectful and character-driven rather than generalised. Early in the summer season, Mark’s clothing might reflect a tentative, not yet fully expressed identity. As the season reaches its peak — the moment of revelation with his parents — costume choices can carry the weight of that honesty: a clarity and simplicity of dress that signals that a decision has been made. The silhouette matters: a costume that fits the body honestly communicates something very different from one that is performing concealment.

Imagine a scene in the winter garden in which Bob tends the rose bush alone before Rosie arrives to speak with him. As a lighting designer, you would begin with the winter state established earlier: a cold, blue-white wash from a single overhead Fresnel, shadows long and hard, the gobo withdrawn so that only bare, flat light reaches the stage. The rose bush itself — a physical set element, bare-stemmed in winter — is lit separately by a downstage floor birdies unit with a pale amber gel, so that it glows slightly warmer than the space around it: still alive, still present. Bob is in the garden’s main wash. When Rosie enters from the kitchen side, the kitchen’s interior warm light briefly spills into the garden area before the door closes: a cross-fade that registers her arrival as a change in the light. As a sound designer, you would fade the winter soundscape (a low wind underscore, near-silence) to near-nothing as their conversation begins, so that the words land in absolute acoustic clarity. As a costume designer, Bob wears a heavier, darker jacket — navy or charcoal — and Rosie’s winter coat in a contrasting lighter fabric: they are the same family, but the visual contrast of their costumes keeps them subtly individualised. Every design choice in this moment supports the emotional content: the coldness of the season, the fragility of the rose, the weight of what has not yet been said.
exam_tip_html:
For the 8-mark ‘Interpret as Designer’ question, the most common error is describing design ideas in general terms: “I would use dark lighting to create a sad mood.” This will not reach the top band. You must name specific elements: which lantern (profile, Fresnel, floor birdie), which colour (gel number or descriptive name — amber, cool blue, steel grey), at what intensity, from which direction, and what specific effect this creates for the audience at a named moment. The mark scheme rewards concreteness. “I would use a tight profile spot with a pale amber gel overhead at steep angle to suggest the harsh Australian sun in the summer garden scene, creating a sense of exposure that mirrors the character’s emotional vulnerability” is the kind of answer that earns Mastering marks.

For the 20-mark extended staging response, spread your answer across multiple design disciplines: set, lighting, sound AND costume. If you focus only on lighting, you are missing a significant portion of the marks. Each discipline should address the same named moment from a different angle, and you should explain how the design choices work together to create a unified effect on the audience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The kitchen and the garden must coexist on a shared stage with clearly distinct qualities: the kitchen is practical and enclosed; the garden is open, symbolic and emotionally loaded. Set, lighting and sound all play a role in maintaining this distinction.
  • The seasonal arc (spring to winter) gives the lighting designer a structural palette: warm, high and bright in spring and summer; colder, flatter and more stripped by autumn and winter. A gobo can track this arc without any physical scene change.
  • Sound design uses two distinct environments: a seasonal soundscape for the garden (cicadas, wind, near-silence) and a minimal or diegetic domestic acoustic for the kitchen. Costume reflects both naturalistic character and the seasonal passage of time, with Mark’s arc demanding particular sensitivity and specificity.

practice_questions.text: Name one type of lantern a lighting designer might use to create a focused special on a performer in a garden scene.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: profile lantern / profile spot / Fresnel / floor birdie. Accept any named lantern type.

practice_questions.text: What is a gobo in lighting design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a gobo as a template inserted into a profile lantern; 1 mark for explaining that it projects a pattern of light onto the stage (e.g. leaf-break, branch pattern, geometric shapes) to suggest environment or texture.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of using a seasonal soundscape in the garden scenes of Things I Know to Be True. How might changing this soundscape across the four seasons contribute to the audience's experience?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the garden soundscape (cicadas, birdsong, wind, near-silence across the seasons); 1 mark for explaining the effect on audience at one or more specific seasonal points (e.g. summer cicadas communicate warmth and outdoor life; winter near-silence communicates coldness and exposure); 1 mark for connecting the soundscape to the emotional arc (the audience unconsciously reads the change in sound as the play's temperature dropping); 1 mark for a specific design choice (e.g. fading the soundscape to silence during the most charged dialogue moments to give the words acoustic clarity).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer working on Things I Know to Be True, explain how you would design the lighting for the winter garden to communicate the emotional state of a parent confronting a revelation they were not prepared for. Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific design choices named for the winter garden: a cold, blue-white wash (Fresnel or wash bar, cool blue gel, reduced intensity compared to earlier seasons); the rose bush lit separately with a small warm unit (floor birdie, pale amber) to suggest it remains alive despite the cold; a profile special on the parent at the moment of confrontation (narrow beam, directed from above, cool white gel) to isolate them from the garden space. Every choice explained with specific effect on the audience at that moment. Silhouette considered: the parent standing still in the stark light, exposed.

Secure: At least two named lighting choices with some specification (lantern type or colour); both linked to the named moment; effect on audience mostly present. May not name all lantern types but shows understanding of how light creates meaning.

Developing: Lighting ideas present but generic ('cold blue light', 'bright spotlight'); one or two choices described without named elements; effect implied rather than explained.

Emerging: Basic mention of lighting with no named elements; no clear link to the named moment or the audience's experience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a set designer might use the coexistence of the kitchen and the garden on a shared stage to communicate the relationship between practicality and emotion in the Price family. Consider specific set elements and their symbolic function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of the kitchen/garden contrast as a spatial metaphor: the kitchen as Fran's domain of direct speech and practical action; the garden as Bob's private emotional territory. Specific set elements discussed (kitchen table and chairs, rose bush, earth ground cloth, levels); the symbolic function of the garden as Bob's inner life. The student analyses what Bovell and the designer want the audience to understand about the Price family's emotional geography. No plot summary.

Secure: Identifies both spaces and their contrasting qualities; explains the garden's symbolic function; names one or two specific set elements; some analysis of audience effect.

Developing: Describes the two spaces without sustained analysis of their symbolic relationship; may mention the rose bush but treat it as literal rather than symbolic.

Emerging: Basic description of the two spaces with little or no analysis of meaning or designer intention.

practice_questions.text: As a designer working across all four design disciplines for a production of Things I Know to Be True, explain how you would use set, lighting, sound and costume to communicate the progression from the spring opening to the winter ending of the play. Refer to specific design choices at two or more points in the seasonal arc and explain the intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All four disciplines addressed across at least two seasonal moments. Set: specific elements for spring (rose bush in bloom, warm kitchen) vs winter (bare stems, stripped stage). Lighting: spring warm amber wash with gobo leaf-break vs winter cold blue-white Fresnel, gobo withdrawn. Sound: spring cicadas and birdsong vs winter near-silence or low wind underscore. Costume: lighter fabrics and warmer colours in spring/summer vs heavier, darker clothing in autumn/winter. Every choice anchored to the named seasonal moment with explanation of intended audience effect. Choices shown to work together as a unified design concept.

Secure: At least three of four disciplines addressed; at least two seasonal moments referenced; most choices specific (one or two named elements per discipline); audience effect mostly present.

Developing: Relevant design ideas across at least two disciplines; seasonal arc acknowledged but choices tend to be generic (e.g. 'warmer lighting in spring'); effect on audience implied not stated.

Emerging: List of design ideas with limited or no justification; one discipline or one season only; mostly descriptive.

knowledge_checks.q: Which set element is a recurring symbol of Bob's emotional life in Things I Know to Be True?
options: The rose bush in the garden

knowledge_checks.q: What is a gobo in theatre lighting design?
options: A type of Fresnel lantern used for general cover
A metal or glass template inserted into a profile lantern to project a pattern
A type of sound effect used to create atmosphere
A gel that changes the colour of a lighting wash

knowledge_checks.q: The background music that plays beneath dialogue without drawing attention to itself is called an _____.
The overall outline and shape created by a costume on the body, used to signal character and emotional state, is called the _____.
Match each design element to the space or season it is most associated with in Things I Know to Be True:
right: Winter season and the play's ending
Spring or summer garden suggesting organic, dappled light

flashcard_questions.q: What is set design in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: The physical organisation of the stage: platforms, furniture, scenic elements and materials.
The quality, colour and intensity of all active lights on stage at a given moment.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a profile lantern used for?
flashcard_questions.a: Producing a hard-edged, focused beam for tight specials and isolating performers.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a Fresnel lantern used for?
flashcard_questions.a: Producing a soft-edged wash of light, used for general cover and warm fill.
A template inserted into a profile lantern to project a pattern onto the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an underscore in sound design?
flashcard_questions.a: Background music beneath dialogue that supports emotional tone without drawing attention.
A continuous layer of ambient sound built from multiple elements to create place and atmosphere.

flashcard_questions.q: What is silhouette in costume design?
flashcard_questions.a: The overall outline and shape a garment creates on the body.

flashcard_questions.q: What are levels in set design?
flashcard_questions.a: Raised or lowered areas of the stage used to create visual interest and organise the space.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two main playing spaces in Things I Know to Be True?
flashcard_questions.a: The kitchen (Fran's domestic interior) and the rose garden (Bob's emotional territory).

flashcard_questions.q: How might a lighting designer signal the move from spring to winter in this play?
flashcard_questions.a: Shift from a warm amber wash to a cold blue-white Fresnel cover at reduced intensity.

flashcard_questions.q: What sound element establishes the Australian summer garden in Things I Know to Be True?
flashcard_questions.a: Cicadas and birdsong as a seasonal outdoor soundscape.

glossary_terms.definition: The way a stage is physically organised, including platforms, levels, furniture and architectural elements, to create environment and control where the audience looks.
The use of raised or lowered areas of the stage to create visual interest, suggest status and organise the playing space.
The quality, colour and intensity of light on stage at a given moment, created by the combination of all active lanterns.
A lantern that produces a hard-edged, focused beam of light, used for sharp specials and tight isolation of performers.
A type of lantern that produces a soft-edged, diffused wash of light, used for general cover and for warm fill.
A metal or glass template inserted into a profile lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage or a surface.
A continuous layer of ambient sound constructed from multiple recorded or live elements to create atmosphere or place.
Background music that plays beneath dialogue or action, supporting the emotional tone without drawing attention to itself.
The overall outline and shape created by a garment on the body, used to signal character, period and emotional state.
